title: Introduction
text: TerminalVibes · learn by doing Your first command. Right here. A terminal is a place to give your computer written instructions. Let’s try one. No install, account, or experience needed.

title: Keyboard Workshop
text: Esc, then B or F is another way; on a Mac, Option may need terminal configuration. Remove the next word Alt+D Remove the word after the cursor. Esc, then D also works in this workshop. Finish a name Tab The playground completes command or file names and shows choices when more than one matches. Find an older command Ctrl+R In your terminal, type a remembered piece; press Ctrl+R again for an older match, Enter to run, or Ctrl+C to cancel. Browsers may take this key to reload the page. Clear the view Ctrl+L Redraw the terminal. Files and command history stay. Browsers may take this key for the address bar; try the clear command in a playground instead. One difference worth knowing: Bash normally uses Ctrl+U to remove text before the cursor. zsh normally removes the whole line. Ctrl+E, then Ctrl+U works for a single line in both. Compare Ctrl+U here Bash default zsh default Ctrl+D has a different job: it can close a shell at an empty prompt. It is not the shortcut for cancelling a command. Try it in your own terminal later: type echo blue without pressing Enter. Use Ctrl+W, type green , then press Enter. You should see green . Repeat once with the guide closed.

title: Keyboard Workshop
text: A browser demonstration is useful; your own keyboard is where the habit grows. Keep going Small skills, useful things. Next, get comfortable reading a reply and asking for help. Then we’ll find folders, make a notebook, and work with your files. Continue to Part 1 Curious about the words and the tools? Open any of these. You can come back later.

title: Intro · What Is the Terminal?
text: What are the terminal and the shell? The terminal is the window you type in. The shell is the program that reads your command and arranges for it to run. You just used echo to print a message. Later, a command might list files, search a notebook, or start a program. Some commands print a reply. Others change something without printing text; we’ll learn how to check what happened. You type A command → The shell runs it An action → You see The result Bash and zsh are two common shells. They share many commands, but some rules and shortcuts differ. This site’s practice terminals simulate part of Bash. They don’t run programs on your computer. You may also hear command line , meaning this way of working by typing instructions, or CLI , short for command-line interface. You do not need to memorize the labels to keep going.

title: Intro · Anatomy of a Prompt
text: What is a prompt? Which text do I type? The prompt marks the place where you can type your next command. In the practice terminal, it is the small arrow beside the input. Your own terminal may show your name, a folder, and a symbol such as $ or % . The prompt is already there. You do not type or copy it. In this course, command examples and results are labeled separately: echo "Hello, world!" Hello, world! The Copy button copies only the command in this example. The text beneath it is the result to look for, not another instruction. Type → Press Enter → Read the result → Try again A # inside a shell example can introduce a comment : a note for the reader that the shell ignores. It does not mean “the computer’s reply.” We will introduce other symbols when you need them.

title: Intro · Your Machine's Terminal
text: Can I use the terminal on my own computer? Yes. You can also complete the first lessons entirely in this browser. When you want to try a real terminal, Part 1 walks through opening yours . On a Mac, Terminal is already in Applications → Utilities. It usually starts zsh. On Linux, look for Terminal in your application menu; the shell depends on your setup. On Windows, this course’s commands need a Bash environment such as WSL or Git Bash. Windows Terminal is the window; its PowerShell tab uses a different command language. You can postpone setup and keep practising here. The browser playground is a learning model, not a complete operating system. Commands such as package installs and network requests use simulated data here. Later lessons identify the steps to repeat on your own computer.

title: Intro · Why Written Commands?
text: Why do people still type commands? A written instruction can be repeated, changed, shared, or connected to another instruction. That is useful when you need to rename many files, find one line in a large log, or repeat a task tomorrow. Modern shells grew out of Unix, developed at Bell Labs starting in 1969. People connected small programs so that the result from one became the input to the next. You will try this idea yourself when we reach pipes . You do not have to replace your everyday apps. Use the terminal when it makes a task easier. The aim is to gain another useful way to work. Open practice terminal Experiment with simulated files. Ask the course helper Get a hint or a smaller explanation. Explore the course map

title: Part 1 · First Contact
text: You can already make the terminal say something. Now let’s get comfortable with the conversation: give an instruction, read the reply, and ask for help when you need it. If you landed here first, try the opening command . The keyboard workshop shows how to move around a line, remove a word, and start again without retyping everything.

title: 1.1 Opening Your Terminal
text: You can do this lesson in the practice terminal below. When you are ready to repeat it on your own computer, choose your system here. On a phone or tablet, keep using the browser practice. macOS: open the Terminal app Hold Command and tap Space to open Spotlight. Type Terminal , then press Enter . A window opens with some text and a cursor. Click in it and try the same echo command you used here. You can also find Terminal in Applications → Utilities. It usually opens a shell called zsh. These first commands work in both zsh and Bash; we’ll point out differences where they matter. Linux: find Terminal in your apps Open your application menu and search for Terminal or Console . On many desktops, Ctrl+Alt+T opens it directly. Click in the window and try your echo command. Windows: choose a Bash terminal Already have Ubuntu or another WSL distribution? Open it from Start, or choose it from Windows Terminal’s tab menu. If you installed Git for Windows instead, open Git Bash from Start. Neither installed? You can keep learning in this browser and do setup later. WSL adds a Linux environment to Windows.

title: 1.1 Opening Your Terminal
text: The official WSL installation guide explains the requirements, installation, restart, and first-time username setup. The usual installation command is below. It is a one-time setup step in PowerShell opened as administrator , not a command to practise in our sandbox: Optional Windows setup · PowerShell as administrator wsl --install After setup, open the Linux terminal for the rest of this course. PowerShell and Command Prompt are useful shells too, but their commands follow different rules. A real terminal works with real files. The embedded practice terminals use their own simulated files. Keep track of which window you are using; this lesson’s commands only ask questions or print text.

title: 1.2 Your First Commands
text: Type one command at a time. Press Enter to run it, then read what appeared. The line where you type is called the prompt . A new prompt means the shell is ready for another instruction. Start with a message you choose. Change the words between the quotes: echo "My garden notebook" My garden notebook echo prints text. The message above is the computer’s reply to the command, so you do not type that second line yourself. Ask for your username whoami You type It prints the name of the account running the command. Here that name is vibe . On your computer it may be different. Ask for the date and time date You type It prints a date and time. The format and time zone depend on the computer, so your result need not match someone else’s. One more question will matter throughout the course: where am I working? Type pwd . It prints your current folder’s location. In this sandbox it begins as /home/vibe . Part 2 will make that location concrete with a folder map. Try it: a short conversation Try a message, your username, the time, and your location below. You can change the examples. The file tree is a picture of this practice terminal’s files; you do not need to use it yet.

title: 1.2 Your First Commands
text: A typo is something you can repair ecoh "hello" bash: ecoh: command not found This message names ecoh because the shell could not find a command with that spelling. It did not run echo . Press ↑ to recall the line, fix the spelling, and press Enter again. If you want to abandon a line before running it, press Ctrl+C . If the screen is crowded, run clear . Clearing the display does not delete your files or your command history. How much older output remains available depends on the terminal.

title: 1.3 Getting Help
text: You do not need to memorize every command. A useful skill is finding just the piece of help you need. Imagine a notebook with many lines. You want to see only the beginning. A command named head does that. Before using it, look up its instructions: man head Open the manual for head man is short for manual. Read the description, then look for -n : it chooses how many lines to show. This extra setting is called an option . We want three lines, so we write -n 3 . head What to do -n 3 How many lines garden-notes.txt Which file On your own computer, a manual usually opens in a reader: use the arrow keys to move, then press q to return to your prompt. In this sandbox, the manual prints directly into the terminal. Try it: find one useful option The practice terminal has a file called garden-notes.txt ready for you. Read man head , then display its first three lines. The file stays unchanged. What if a command has no manual? Many programs accept --help to print a shorter guide. It is common, but not universal. For example, some versions of ls accept it and others do not. Bash also has commands built into the shell. For those, try help followed by the name, such as help cd .

title: 1.3 Getting Help
text: In zsh, built-in help works differently. The course cheatsheet and a program’s official documentation are useful alternatives. In this sandbox , help on its own lists the commands it supports. If an otherwise valid command is missing here, that is a simulator limitation, not a mistake you made. Try looking something up with less help The closing practice uses ls , a command that lists names in a folder. Some names begin with a dot and are usually hidden. Read man ls to find how to include them. You can inspect, read, and retry as often as you need. You now have a way to try a command, repair a typo, and look up an option. Next: find your way around folders →

title: Part 2 · Moving Around
text: Let’s make a home for a little garden notebook. Before we create anything, we need to know where it will go. A terminal has a current folder . Commands that use a short name, such as notes.txt , look for that name there. In terminal instructions, a folder is also called a directory . The two words mean the same thing here. pwd Find your location ls Look around cd Choose a folder

title: 2.1 Where Am I?
text: Imagine opening a file manager. It shows a folder’s name and what is inside. In a terminal, we ask those two questions separately. pwd /home/vibe Where am I working? pwd means “print working directory.” This answer is the location of your current folder. Here, it is the home folder of an account named vibe . Your own computer may show something like /Users/sam or /home/sam instead. ls documents notes.txt projects What is in this folder? · example result ls lists names. A name might belong to a file or to a folder containing more names. Colors can help distinguish them, but colors depend on the terminal’s settings. We won’t rely on color alone. Find names that a normal listing leaves out A name starting with a dot is usually omitted by ls . Add the option -a to include it: ls -a . .. .bashrc .config documents notes.txt projects These hidden names often hold settings. Hidden does not mean locked or secret; it is a display convention. The special entries . and .. mean “this folder” and “its parent.” We will use them shortly. Read a longer listing ls -l notes.txt -rw-r--r-- 1 vibe staff 118 Jul 12 08:30 notes.txt Start at the right: the name, then the date, then the size in bytes.

title: 2.1 Where Am I?
text: A byte is a unit of stored data; one written character can use more than one byte. The first character is - for a regular file or d for a directory. Part 5 explains the other permission letters. ls -lh formats larger sizes as values such as 4.2K . ls -la combines the long listing with hidden names. For this command, -la is shorthand for -l -a ; option letters belong to each individual command.

title: 2.2 Paths
text: A path tells a command where to find something. Read the slashes as steps between folders. Here is a small example tree: The full address of the note is /home/vibe/garden/notes.txt . Start at the first slash, called the root directory , then follow home , vibe , and garden to the file. Kind of path Example Where it starts Absolute /home/vibe/garden/notes.txt The root, regardless of your current folder Relative garden/notes.txt Your current folder; correct here if you are in /home/vibe Relative notes.txt Your current folder; correct here if you are in /home/vibe/garden A useful prediction: if you move into photos , will notes.txt still name the note? No: that short name now refers to something inside photos. Use ../notes.txt to go up one level before choosing the file. Shortcut Meaning Example / The root directory /home/vibe ~ Your home directory ~/garden . Your current directory ./notes.txt .. The parent directory ../notes.txt One name can contain a space The shell normally uses spaces to separate the pieces of a command. To keep My Notes together as one name, put quotes around it: cd "My Notes" One folder name, including its space cd My Notes supplies two separate names.

title: 2.2 Paths
text: The quotes are instructions to the shell; they are not part of the folder’s name. A backslash can protect a single space too: cd My\ Notes . Try typing the first few letters of a name, then pressing Tab . In many shells, completion fills in a matching name. If several names match, type another letter or press Tab again to see choices. The keyboard workshop gives you a place to practise this without a long command to manage. Single quotes, double quotes, and literal text Both 'My Notes' and "My Notes" keep the space inside the name. Single quotes preserve their contents literally. Double quotes also allow variable values such as $HOME to expand; we will use variables in Part 5. Keep the home shortcut outside quotes: ~/"My Notes" works. "~/My Notes" treats the tilde as an ordinary character in a real shell. Later, "$HOME/My Notes" will give you a convenient quoted form.

title: 2.3 Changing Directories
text: cd changes your current folder. It does not move the files themselves. Try a move, then ask pwd where you landed: cd garden pwd ls In the example tree above · run one line at a time After this move, pwd would show /home/vibe/garden . If a folder called garden does not exist in your current practice, choose a name you can see with ls instead. Command What changes cd .. Go to the parent folder. cd ~ Go home. Plain cd does this too. cd - Return to the previous working folder. ls photos Look inside photos without changing your location. If cd reports “No such file or directory,” your location has not changed. Check pwd , list the names, then correct the path. If it says “Not a directory,” you may have chosen a file. If it says “Permission denied,” the folder exists but your account cannot enter it; Part 5 explains that case. Each shell has its own current folder. Moving in one terminal tab does not move another tab. This is why checking your location is useful even when you were “just there.” Try it: find the hidden garden note Explore the seeded folders below with pwd , ls , and cd . Use ls -a if a clue seems missing.

title: 2.3 Changing Directories
text: When you find the note, cat followed by its filename prints its contents—we’ll practise reading files in more detail below.

title: 2.4 Making Things
text: mkdir makes a directory. touch creates an empty file if that name does not already exist. Start with one folder, then put one file inside it: mkdir garden-notebook cd garden-notebook touch plan.md ls A notebook folder and its first empty file The final listing should include plan.md . The .md ending is a common name for a Markdown text file. It is still a text file; the ending does not put anything inside it. Now make a few places to organize the notebook: mkdir notes recipes photos touch notes/seeds.txt notes/weather.txt ls notes Create names, then check where they landed These commands usually print nothing when they finish successfully. That is why we use ls to inspect the result. Silence alone is not the check. Create missing parent folders mkdir photos/spring/week-1 fails if photos/spring does not exist. mkdir -p photos/spring/week-1 creates the missing parents too. The -p form also accepts a directory that already exists. It can still fail if you lack permission or a file is blocking the path. Running touch plan.md again keeps the file’s contents and updates its timestamps. It does not empty the file.

title: 2.4 Making Things
text: To inspect a whole small tree, try ls -R garden-notebook from its parent; the capital R asks for a listing inside subfolders too. Try it: keep a name with a space together The next sandbox contains My Projects . Enter that folder with a quoted path, create an empty file called shipped.txt , and list the folder to check. “Shipped” is just the chosen filename; no software is being published.

title: 2.5 Looking Inside Files
text: cat prints a file and gives your prompt back. Use it for something short: cat notes.txt Water the seedlings. Check the sunny windowsill. Example: a note with two lines Reading an empty file prints nothing. It has no text yet. Reading a photograph with cat is not useful: image files are not ordinary text. A filename is a clue, not proof of its contents. Try it: add a seed to the notebook In the next practice, run cat notes/seeds.txt to read the list. Choose Edit a file , open notes/seeds.txt , and add thyme on a new line after basil and mint. Save the file, then run cat again to check the saved result. The editor and this terminal share the same simulated files. Typing in the editor changes the draft; saving changes the file. Reading it with cat confirms what the terminal will actually see. Write a note on your own computer This is a real-terminal practice ; the embedded sandbox does not provide nano. In a practice folder you created on your computer, run: nano plan.md Open or create a text file in nano Type Plant basil by the window. Hold Ctrl and press O to save (“Write Out”). Check that the filename says plan.md , then press Enter . Press Ctrl+X to leave the editor.

title: 2.5 Looking Inside Files
text: Run cat plan.md and check that your sentence is there. In nano’s help bar, ^O means Ctrl+O. If nano asks whether to save changed text when you exit, Y saves and N discards those unsaved edits. If nano is unavailable, use your usual editor in plain-text mode and save into the same practice folder. Try a variation: open the note again, add a second line, save, exit, and read it back. The skill is the complete loop, including checking the saved file. Read longer text without losing your place On your own computer, less notes.txt opens a reader. Use Space for the next page, b for the previous page, and / followed by a word and Enter to search. n finds the next match. Press q to leave. Our sandbox prints less output directly rather than opening a full-screen reader. Need Use The whole short file cat notes.txt The first three lines head -n 3 notes.txt The last three lines tail -n 3 notes.txt A live view as a log grows (real terminal) tail -f app.log ; stop with Ctrl+C If you accidentally opened Vim Press Esc , type :q! , then press Enter to leave without saving your changes. To save and leave, use :wq instead.

title: 2.5 Looking Inside Files
text: These are instructions inside Vim , not commands to type at an ordinary shell prompt. Try it: build your notebook workspace Make the folders and empty files described in the practice below. Inspect each folder before continuing. These files start empty. Open one with Edit a file if you want to add a note, then read it back with cat. Part 4 will show another way to write files: saving a command’s output. Before moving on, explain this in your own words: why can the same notes.txt command name a different file after cd ? Next, we will copy, rename, and organize the files you can now find.

title: Part 3 · Copy, Move, Delete
text: Your notebook has a draft, some photographs, and a few files you no longer need. Let’s organize them, one small change at a time. There are three different actions to keep separate. cp makes a copy. mv moves or renames the original. rm removes a name without putting it in the Trash. We’ll inspect the result after each action.

title: 3.1 Copying
text: Before changing a note, make a second copy you can return to. Read this command as “copy plan.md to plan-original.md.” The source comes first; the destination comes last. cp plan.md plan-original.md ls cat plan-original.md In a folder containing plan.md · copy, list, read The first command normally prints nothing. The listing should now contain both names, and cat should print the copied text. Editing plan.md afterward does not update this separate copy. The destination can be a new name or an existing folder mkdir copies cp plan.md copies/ ls copies Copy into an existing folder, keeping the filename Here the copied file is copies/plan.md . The final slash makes your intention easy to read. The destination folder must exist; cp does not create missing parent folders. Check the destination first. A normal copy can replace an existing destination file. On your own computer, cp -i plan.md copies/ asks before overwriting. Answer n if you are unsure. In this sandbox, -i refuses an overwrite and explains the prompt rather than running a yes/no conversation.

title: 3.1 Copying
text: Copy a folder and what is inside it cp -R notes notes-copy ls notes-copy Create notes-copy when that destination does not already exist The capital -R means copy recursively: include the folder’s contents and its subfolders. -r also works for these examples. Without a recursive option, cp normally refuses a directory. Whether the destination already exists matters. If notes-copy is absent, the command creates it as the copy. If it is already a directory, the source may be copied inside it, producing notes-copy/notes . Check with ls before repeating a folder-copy command. Try a variation: copy one short note, edit only the copy with the file editor, and read both names with cat. You should see two different versions. What makes a useful backup? A nearby copy is useful before an edit. It does not protect you from losing the disk, or from deleting both copies together. Keep important work in a backup system with separate storage and retained versions. A filename ending in .bak is only a convention; the name itself does not protect the file.

title: 3.2 Moving & Renaming
text: Renaming a file is a move to a new name in the same folder. Moving it to another folder uses the same command: mv rough-notes.txt planting-plan.txt mkdir finished mv planting-plan.txt finished/ ls ls finished Rename, then move · start with a disposable rough-notes.txt After the rename, the original name is gone. After the move, the file is inside finished. Its text has not been rewritten. This makes mv different from cp: you have relocated the file, not created a second independent copy. You can move several sources into one existing folder: mv basil.jpg mint.jpg photos/ Two files, one destination folder With several sources, the final argument must be a directory that already exists. If you see “No such file or directory,” check both sides: a source may be misspelled, or the destination’s parent may be missing. mv -i asks before overwriting an existing destination file on a real terminal. Our sandbox refuses that overwrite instead. Choose a new destination name when you want to preserve both versions. Moving a whole folder does not require -R. A move within one filesystem is often quick because the system changes its location rather than copying all its contents.

title: 3.2 Moving & Renaming
text: Moving between disks requires copying data and removing the source after that succeeds; let it finish and inspect the result. To undo a simple rename or move, move the file back—provided nothing else has taken its old place. If a move overwrote another file, renaming it back does not recover the overwritten contents. That is what a backup or version history is for.

title: 3.3 Deleting (Carefully)
text: rm removes files without moving them to your file manager’s Trash. Treat deletion as permanent unless you have a separate backup. The playground’s Undo button is a learning feature; an ordinary shell does not provide it. Start with a disposable file you made yourself. This sequence creates one, shows it, removes it, then checks the folder: touch practice-scrap.txt ls practice-scrap.txt rm practice-scrap.txt ls One deliberately disposable file The last listing should no longer include practice-scrap.txt. You did not need a force option or a wildcard to remove one known file. Task Command shape What to expect Remove one file rm scrap.txt It removes the named file. Remove an empty folder rmdir empty-folder It refuses if the folder is not empty. Remove a folder and its contents rm -r old-drafts Inspect the folder first; its contents are targets too. Ask before removing (real terminal) rm -i scrap.txt Read the question and answer y or n. The sandbox leaves it untouched. A short routine before removing a folder pwd ls -la old-drafts ls -R old-drafts Inspection only · choose your actual disposable folder Confirm where you are and what is inside the intended folder, including hidden names.

title: 3.3 Deleting (Carefully)
text: If you are undecided, move it to a clearly named review folder instead of deleting it today. When you have decided to remove it, use the same explicit path in rm -r old-drafts . The option -f suppresses questions and ignores missing-file errors. It does not grant permission and does not make a command correct. The common combination rm -rf asks for recursive removal without questions; there is no reason to make that your default for a single scrap file. If a filename starts with a dash A name such as -old.txt can look like options. An explicit path avoids that ambiguity: rm ./-old.txt names a file in this folder. Commands such as rm also accept -- to end options: rm -- -old.txt . Check a tool’s help before assuming it supports that convention. Try it: sort the downloads Move the photos and invoices into their destination folders. Read the filenames before deciding which installer is no longer needed. Check both the source and destination after each move.

title: 3.4 Wildcards
text: Sometimes you want every photo with a certain name, not one photo at a time. A wildcard pattern , also called a glob, selects matching filenames. Pattern Matches Does not match *.txt notes.txt, plan.txt photo.jpg photo-?.jpg photo-1.jpg, photo-a.jpg photo-12.jpg note-[12].txt note-1.txt, note-2.txt note-3.txt * matches any number of characters within a path component, including none. ? matches one character. Brackets choose one character from a set. The pattern is about names; it does not inspect what the files contain. echo *.txt You type a pattern echo notes.txt plan.txt The shell supplies matching names notes.txt plan.txt echo prints its arguments echo *.txt notes.txt plan.txt A simple preview · example matching names The shell expands the unquoted pattern before running the command. So echo can show a simple selection without changing those files. For names containing spaces, a one-name-per-line preview is easier to read: printf '%s\n' ./*.txt Show each matching name on its own line printf is another printing command. Here, %s means print one supplied string and \n means start a new line. The format repeats for each matching name.

title: 3.4 Wildcards
text: The ./ prefix makes the names explicit paths in the current folder. After inspecting a selection, you can use it with a copying or moving command. For example, cp ./*.txt copies/ copies matching text files into an existing copies folder. Rerun the preview if the directory or its files have changed. Two differences to recognize By default, a star does not include names beginning with a dot. Use ls -a to inspect hidden names separately. Also, photos/*.jpg selects files directly inside photos, not inside every subfolder. Recursive glob features exist, but differ by shell and settings; find gives us an explicit way to search a whole tree. If nothing matches: Bash normally leaves the pattern unchanged, so a command may receive the literal text *.txt . zsh normally stops with “no matches found.” Neither message means the files were deleted. List the folder, check the pattern, and try again. Our sandbox uses the Bash-style default. Braces make words; globs find existing names In Bash and zsh, mkdir -p notes/{spring,summer} expands to two folder names even if neither exists. Braces generate words; globs match names already present.

title: 3.4 Wildcards
text: The longer form mkdir -p notes/spring notes/summer is equally valid and often easier to read. Try it: choose exactly the right files Preview each pattern before using it to move or remove anything. Some similar names are deliberate distractions. It is fine to list them several times while you decide. Check your understanding: what changes if the last argument to cp is an existing directory instead of a new filename? Next, we’ll work with the text inside files.

title: Part 4 · Text & Pipes
text: A folder full of notes is useful. Being able to ask “which notes mention basil?” or “how many times did this happen?” is more useful still. We’ll start by saving one message into a file. Then we’ll send text through small tools: one finds matching lines, another counts them, another sorts them. Build each step separately so you can see what changes.

title: 4.1 Redirection
text: So far, echo has printed to the terminal. Put > and a filename after it to send that text into a file instead: echo "Water the basil" > garden-tasks.txt No message appeared because the text went into garden-tasks.txt. Check the saved file: cat garden-tasks.txt Water the basil This is redirection : choosing where output goes. If the named file does not exist, the shell creates it. If it already exists, > normally empties it before the command runs. Use a new filename when you want to preserve the earlier contents. Add another line without replacing the first echo "Check the mint" >> garden-tasks.txt cat garden-tasks.txt Append a task, then read both lines The double arrow >> appends. You should now see Water the basil followed by Check the mint. Try a third task of your own. Pause and predict: what would happen if you used a single arrow for the third task? The earlier tasks would be replaced. A longer symbol is not “more powerful” here; it is a different instruction. Keep normal results and errors separate A command can print useful results and an error in the same run. Those messages travel through two channels: standard output for results and standard error for diagnostics.

title: 4.1 Redirection
text: A normal > redirects only standard output. The next example names a file that exists and one that does not. First run it without redirection so you can see both kinds of reply: ls garden-tasks.txt missing.txt One existing file, one deliberately missing file Now keep the replies in different files. 2> redirects the error channel, numbered 2: ls garden-tasks.txt missing.txt > found.txt 2> errors.txt cat found.txt cat errors.txt Separate the listing from the error The listing belongs in found.txt; the missing-file message belongs in errors.txt. The error is still a real failure. Saving the message did not fix its cause. Try it: capture both replies In this practice, app.log exists and ghost.log does not. List both, save the normal listing as found.txt and the diagnostic as errors.txt, then read both files. Input redirection and merging the two output channels Standard input , numbered 0, is where a program reads incoming data. sort < names.txt makes a file that input. The other channels are standard output (1) and standard error (2). > all.log 2>&1 first directs normal output to all.log, then directs errors to the same destination.

title: 4.1 Redirection
text: Order matters: the redirections are applied left to right. 2>&1 > all.log sends errors to the output’s earlier destination, so it is different. Do not read a file and redirect into that same file in one command. For example, sort names.txt > names.txt can empty the source before sort reads it. Write to a different filename, inspect the result, then deliberately replace the original if needed.

title: 4.2 Pipes
text: An arrow sends output to a file. A pipe , written | , sends one command’s standard output to the next command’s standard input. Try this small example. printf prints three lines; sort arranges them alphabetically: printf '%s\n' mint basil thyme | sort basil mint thyme printf Produces the lines | Passes the text along sort Reads and orders the lines Without the pipe, printf would print to your terminal. With it, sort receives the text and prints the final result. The left command’s output is not automatically also shown on screen. Add one more stage to ask how many lines remain: printf '%s\n' mint basil thyme | sort | wc -l 3 wc -l counts newline characters. Here each item ends in a newline, so the answer is three lines. A pipe passes text, not the name of a temporary file. That distinction will matter when we combine file-finding tools later. Watch output and save a copy tee copies its input into a file while also passing it onward. Use it when you want to see the answer and keep it: cat garden-tasks.txt | tee saved-tasks.txt Print the tasks and write the same text into another file tee replaces an existing destination unless you use tee -a to append.

title: 4.2 Pipes
text: Like an ordinary pipe, it receives standard output; errors only join the stream if you explicitly redirect them there. Try a variation: reverse the ordering with sort -r . The count should remain three. A useful check asks what should change and what should stay the same.

title: 4.3 Searching Text
text: grep prints matching lines. To search for text exactly as written, start with -F , meaning fixed text: grep -F 'basil' garden-tasks.txt Water the basil This finds lines containing basil anywhere. It does not mean “only the word basil,” and it does not include Basil unless you add -i to ignore case. No matches normally means no printed lines, not that the file was changed. Need Example Ignore letter case grep -Fi 'basil' garden-tasks.txt Include line numbers grep -Fn 'basil' garden-tasks.txt Keep lines without that text grep -Fv 'mint' garden-tasks.txt Count matching lines grep -Fc 'basil' garden-tasks.txt Search files under a folder grep -Frn 'basil' notes/ A log is a record a program writes as it runs. Many logs label entries INFO, WARN, or ERROR. Searching those words can help you find a problem without reading the whole file. grep -Fn 'ERROR' server.log grep -F 'ERROR' server.log | grep -Fv 'retry' Find error lines, then remove a known repeated message The second command keeps error lines that do not contain retry. Inspect what you excluded as well as what you kept; filtering a message out of a report does not make the problem disappear.

title: 4.3 Searching Text
text: When you need a pattern instead of literal text Without -F, grep uses a regular expression . This is a pattern language for text, different from the filename globs in Part 3. Begin with just two anchors: grep '^Water' garden-tasks.txt grep 'basil$' garden-tasks.txt First: lines starting with Water. Second: lines ending with basil. ^ marks the beginning of a line; $ marks its end. A dot in a regular expression matches a character. A star repeats the pattern item before it. To search for a literal filename such as plan.md , grep -F 'plan.md' file.txt avoids treating the dot as a wildcard. Keep the pattern in quotes so the shell passes it intact. grep '*.txt' is not the way to select text files: grep’s pattern is for contents . A filename glob goes where the filenames go, for example grep -F 'basil' ./*.txt . Try it: read the story of a crash Search the supplied server.log. Start with one useful word, include line numbers, then narrow the result. Read the nearby text before deciding what caused the failure.

title: 4.4 Counting & Shaping
text: A search gives you matching lines. Now we can turn those lines into a count or a short report. Tool Job Detail that matters wc -l Count newline characters A final line without a newline is not counted by -l. sort Order lines Use -n for numeric order, -r to reverse it. uniq -c Count adjacent equal lines Sort first if equal lines are scattered. cut Choose fields separated by one character It does not understand quoted CSV fields. Try it: get one reliable count Find the ERROR lines, pipe them into wc -l , and save the count to the requested file. Check the count against the matching lines themselves. Build a small report one stage at a time Suppose this is the entire content of a tiny access.log. Each line is a request to a website. The first field identifies a network address; GET is the request’s action, and the last field is the requested web path. Example access.log · four requests 203.0.113.9 GET /home 198.51.100.4 GET /about 203.0.113.9 GET /garden 192.0.2.55 GET /home cut -d ' ' -f 1 says: separate fields at spaces and keep field one.

title: 4.4 Counting & Shaping
text: For this deliberately simple format, that field is the address: cut -d ' ' -f 1 access.log 203.0.113.9 198.51.100.4 203.0.113.9 192.0.2.55 Sort those lines to put equal addresses beside one another: cut -d ' ' -f 1 access.log | sort 192.0.2.55 198.51.100.4 203.0.113.9 203.0.113.9 Count each adjacent group with uniq -c: cut -d ' ' -f 1 access.log | sort | uniq -c 1 192.0.2.55 1 198.51.100.4 2 203.0.113.9 Then order by the leading number. sort -n puts the largest count last; sort -nr puts it first. Output may have extra alignment spaces. cut -d ' ' -f 1 access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -n Select the field, group equal values, count, rank The totals should add up to four requests. An address is not necessarily a person: several people can share one network address, and a person can use several addresses. Name the report accurately. Try it: build the report yourself This practice contains a longer log. Run each stage before adding the next. Save the final report as top-visitors.txt and check that the busiest address appears at the bottom. Why a comma is not always a column boundary A simple table such as basil,green,3 is easy to split at commas.

title: 4.4 Counting & Shaping
text: Real CSV can quote a value that contains a comma, a quote, or even a newline. Neither plain cut nor awk -F, parses those CSV rules. Use a CSV-aware tool or library for a general spreadsheet export. Part 7 practises simple tables and explains the boundary.

title: 4.5 Finding Files
text: grep asks “which lines contain this text?” find can ask “where are the files with these names?” It searches a folder and its descendants. find . -type f -name '*.md' Find Markdown filenames under the current folder Read the pieces in order: start at . , keep regular files with -type f , and match their names against '*.md' . The quotes stop the shell from expanding the star before find sees it. find notes -type f -name '*.txt' find . -type d -name 'photos' One search for text files; another for folders named photos Start with the smallest sensible folder. Searching your whole computer creates unnecessary output and permission errors. If nothing matches, check the starting folder, capitalization, and pattern. Searching paths is different from searching their contents find . -name '*.py' | grep TODO searches the printed path names for TODO. It does not open each Python file. To search contents recursively, use grep -rn TODO . ; to limit the file set on a real terminal, find can pass each filename as an argument: find . -type f -name '*.py' -exec grep -n 'TODO' /dev/null {} + Real terminal · search only the Python files find selected -exec runs the following command.

title: 4.5 Finding Files
text: {} marks where the found paths go, and + groups paths into batches. The harmless empty file /dev/null ensures grep sees multiple file arguments and includes filenames in its results. The sandbox does not implement find -exec. Do not use a plain line-based find ... | xargs ... recipe for arbitrary filenames. Spaces, quotes, and newlines can be part of a filename. On a real terminal, -exec passes the names directly. A null-delimited find -print0 | xargs -0 pipeline is another approach, but those options are outside this sandbox. Try it: collect the remaining TODOs The sample project uses Python files ending in .py. Locate them with find, then use grep’s recursive search to collect the TODO lines with their file and line numbers. Save the report as the activity requests. No source files need to change. Explain one pipeline from this part aloud: what does each stage receive, and what does it produce? If one stage is unclear, run it separately. That habit scales to much larger jobs.

title: Part 5 · Permissions & Config
text: A file can exist and still refuse to run. A program can be installed and still be hard for your shell to find. Let’s separate those two problems. Permissions describe what an account may do with a file. The environment supplies named settings to programs. We’ll inspect each before changing it, so a fix has a reason behind it.

title: 5.1 Reading ls -l
text: Ask for a long listing of one file. This example is a small script—a file of commands that we will learn to write in Part 6: ls -l backup.sh -rw-r--r-- 1 vibe staff 214 Jul 12 08:30 backup.sh The owner’s account name is vibe. The group is staff: a named collection of accounts. The letters at the start describe permissions for the owner, the group, and everyone else. - Regular file rw- Owner: read and write r-- Group: read r-- Others: read r permits reading, w permits writing, and x permits executing a file as a program. A dash in one of those positions means that permission is absent. The initial character describes the file type: - for a regular file, d for a directory, or l for a symbolic link. The owner is not necessarily you. Use whoami to check your account and id to see its groups. A process—including an AI agent—usually acts with the account that started it. Merely calling a program an “agent” does not give it a separate restricted account. Directories use the letters differently Permission On a directory Read (r) List the names inside. Execute (x) Traverse the directory to access a named entry; cd needs this.

title: 5.1 Reading ls -l
text: Write (w) Change the directory’s entries, usually together with execute permission. Removing a file usually depends on permissions on its containing directory, not just the file’s own write bit. That is why making a file read-only is not a complete deletion lock. Real systems can also apply access-control lists, sticky bits, and other rules beyond this basic view; the sandbox models only a small part of that system.

title: 5.2 chmod
text: Suppose you try ./backup.sh and see Permission denied. First read the file with cat and inspect it with ls -l backup.sh . If it is the script you intended to run, you own it, and its owner permissions lack x, add that one permission: cat backup.sh ls -l backup.sh chmod u+x backup.sh ls -l backup.sh ./backup.sh Inspect the script, grant owner execution, then try it chmod changes a file’s permission mode. u+x means “add execute for the owner.” It does not mean “make everything readable and writable.” The leading ./ names a file in your current folder explicitly. Form Meaning chmod u+x backup.sh Add owner execute permission. chmod go-w notes.txt Remove group and other write permission. chmod 600 private-notes.txt Set owner read/write; no group or other permission. chmod 644 notes.txt Set owner read/write, group/other read. chmod 755 backup.sh Set owner read/write/execute, group/other read/execute. The numeric forms replace the ordinary permission bits rather than just adding one. Each digit combines read (4), write (2), and execute (1): 6 is 4+2. Choose the intended access; there is no single correct permission for every document or script. You will see chmod +x without an audience.

title: 5.2 chmod
text: On real Unix systems, the current umask influences which permissions may be changed when the audience is omitted. It is not unconditionally identical to a+x . Writing u+x makes our intention clear. Permission denied can have other causes, including a parent folder you cannot traverse or a filesystem that disallows execution. If the listing does not support the missing-x diagnosis, investigate that cause instead. Broad changes such as chmod -R 777 give access to many files and rarely explain or correctly fix the underlying problem. Try it: diagnose the script that will not run Read deploy.sh, inspect its permissions, add owner execution, and run it. “Deploy” here is a simulated task; nothing is published to the internet.

title: 5.3 sudo
text: Some tasks require an administrator’s authority. sudo runs an allowed command as another account, usually the administrator account called root. Your system’s policy decides whether you are allowed to use it. A common example is installing a system package on a Debian or Ubuntu machine. This is a real-machine example, not a setup step required for this lesson: sudo apt install htop Example on Debian/Ubuntu · installs the htop process viewer If sudo asks for your password, the terminal may show no dots or letters while you type. That is normal. Type your account password and press Enter. Read any package changes the installer proposes before accepting them. Do not add sudo automatically after an error. A misspelled path, a missing program, and a missing execute bit are different problems. Running the same mistake with more authority can make a larger unwanted change. Before using it, be able to say what the command will change, why your normal account cannot do that, and whether the path is correct. Administrative access is powerful, but it does not bypass every operating-system protection. The playground does not grant administrator access.

title: 5.3 sudo
text: Native Windows elevation also follows different rules from sudo inside WSL; this section’s Linux command should not be copied into a PowerShell tab.

title: 5.4 Environment Variables
text: A variable is a named value. The shell already has one called HOME containing your home folder’s path. A dollar sign asks for its value: echo "$HOME" /home/vibe Now try one of your own: PLANT="basil" echo "$PLANT" echo "Today I planted $PLANT" Name a value, then use it in a message There are no spaces around = when assigning a shell variable. The name on the left has no dollar sign. The dollar sign is for reading its value later. Double quotes preserve spaces in the resulting value. A newly assigned variable is normally local to this shell. export includes it in the environment given to programs started afterward: export EDITOR=nano echo "$EDITOR" Set a preferred editor for programs that read this setting This does not install nano or change every program’s editor. A program must actually consult EDITOR for it to matter. Assigning a new value to a variable that was already exported keeps it exported. Each program receives a copy of the environment. It cannot change its parent shell’s variables by changing its own copy. A new terminal does not automatically inherit settings you just typed into an unrelated terminal window.

title: 5.4 Environment Variables
text: PATH: the shell’s search list for programs echo "$PATH" type ls which ls Inspect the search path and how ls is resolved PATH contains directory names separated by colons, for example /usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin . For an external command name without a slash, the shell searches those directories. Earlier matches can hide later versions of a program. type also helps reveal shell built-ins and aliases. which is useful for external paths but does not always describe the shell’s full lookup behavior. On a real Bash or zsh terminal, command -v ls is another useful check. If a command is not found, start with its spelling, then ask whether it is installed and whether its directory is on PATH. If you already know the program’s full path, you can run that path directly. A command beginning with ./ does not ask PATH to choose a file for you. export PATH="$PATH:$HOME/.local/bin" Add one directory to this shell’s existing search list Keep the old $PATH on the right. Replacing it with only the new directory can hide ordinary commands. Appending searches the new location last; prepending searches it first. Add a directory you trust, not a shared folder where someone else can replace commands.

title: 5.4 Environment Variables
text: Environment variables can contain credentials. Inspect only the setting you need; do not paste a full env dump into a chat or issue. Use the program’s documented credential setup for real keys. Our practice uses ordinary words such as basil, never real secrets. Try it: find the missing command A small tool named greet exists in the sandbox. Find where it lives and either run its explicit path or add its directory to PATH. Explain why your chosen fix works.

title: 5.5 Your Shell Config
text: An alias is a short name for a command you want to reuse. Try one in the current shell before making it permanent: alias ll='ls -lh' ll alias Create a short listing command, use it, then inspect aliases The quotes keep the longer command together when defining the alias. unalias ll removes this alias from the current shell. A name such as ll is optional shorthand; keep learning the underlying command too. To keep it for future sessions, add its definition to the startup file your shell actually reads. On a real machine, inspect the file first, keep a copy if it already exists, and use your editor to add one line. Do not replace the entire file with the example below. alias ll='ls -lh' One line to add to the appropriate shell startup file Shell session Common personal startup file Interactive zsh ~/.zshrc Interactive Bash that is not a login shell ~/.bashrc Bash login shell A profile such as ~/.bash_profile ; it often loads .bashrc explicitly. zsh login shell ~/.zprofile also runs; interactive sessions still read .zshrc. A new terminal window can start a login or non-login shell, depending on the application’s settings. That is why a setting can work in one terminal but not another.

title: 5.5 Your Shell Config
text: Begin with one alias and test a new window before adding more configuration. What source actually does After editing a trusted file, source ~/.zshrc runs its commands in the current zsh shell. Bash users can use source ~/.bashrc for that file. Read it before sourcing; this executes commands, not just harmless declarations. Running bash script.sh starts a child shell. Its variable changes and current folder do not alter the parent. But files it creates, changes, or deletes do persist . A child shell is not a file-safety sandbox. Sourcing instead applies commands to your current shell, so changes to variables, aliases, and location remain there too. If a new setting breaks your startup, reopen the file in an editor and remove that new line or restore your saved copy. Repeatedly adding more PATH lines makes the problem harder to inspect. Try it: make one useful shortcut Define and use an alias. Then add its definition to the sandbox’s .bashrc without discarding the existing content. Read the file back. In a real terminal you would finally test a fresh shell as well.

title: 5.5 Your Shell Config
text: You can now distinguish “the shell did not find it” from “this account cannot do that.” Next we will save a small routine as a script and make its success or failure explicit.

title: Part 6 · Scripts & Automation
text: You have commands that work. A script lets you save them in a file and run them again. The next step is deciding what should happen when one of those commands fails. We’ll begin with a tiny script in the browser, add arguments and success checks, then practise conditions and loops in real Bash. The browser sandbox runs the simple command sequences shown in its activities; the longer Bash examples are labeled as real-terminal practice.

title: 6.1 Your First Script
text: Create a file named hello.sh with the playground’s Edit a file button, or use nano hello.sh on your own computer. Put these two lines in it and save: #!/usr/bin/env bash echo "The garden notebook is ready" Contents of hello.sh · paste into the file editor The second line is the echo command you already know. The first line, beginning #! , is called a shebang . It tells the system to use Bash when this file is launched directly. /usr/bin/env finds Bash using PATH. Read the saved file before running it, then run it explicitly with Bash: cat hello.sh bash hello.sh Check the file, then ask Bash to run its commands You should see The garden notebook is ready. To run the file directly with ./hello.sh , first add its owner execute permission: chmod u+x hello.sh ./hello.sh Run the same script directly The .sh ending is a helpful filename convention, not what makes it run. Bash can read a script without its execute bit when you explicitly use bash hello.sh ; launching ./hello.sh requires execution permission. Try it: save a small copying routine The activity contains notes.txt. Create backup.sh with Edit a file , paste the following contents, and save.

title: 6.1 Your First Script
text: This first version copies one fixed file; it can replace the same destination on a later run. We will improve that behavior below. #!/usr/bin/env bash mkdir -p "$HOME/backups" cp "$HOME/notes.txt" "$HOME/backups/notes-backup.txt" Contents of backup.sh · first small version Read backup.sh, add owner execution, and run it. Then read ~/backups/notes-backup.txt and compare it with ~/notes.txt . A success message alone would be weaker evidence than seeing the right contents in the right place. Try a variation: change the source note in the file editor, run the script again, and inspect the copied note. This is an update to one copy, not a history of older versions. Running a script starts a child shell. Its local variables and directory changes do not move your parent shell. Files it writes remain changed after the script exits. A script is saved work, not an automatic safety boundary.

title: 6.2 Exit Codes & Chaining
text: A finished command returns a number called its exit status or exit code. Zero means success according to that command’s rules. A nonzero value means another outcome, often failure. false echo "$?" true echo "$?" Run one line at a time · expect 1, then 0 false deliberately returns 1, and true returns 0. Neither prints a message. The special value $? gives the status of the command that just finished. Ask immediately: running another command replaces that status. Nonzero does not always mean a crash. For example, grep uses 1 when no lines match and a different status for an error. Read the command’s documented meanings when that distinction matters. Choose whether the next command runs true && echo "That succeeded" That succeeded false && echo "That succeeded" false || echo "That did not succeed" That did not succeed a && b Run b only if a succeeds a || b Run b only if a does not succeed a ; b Run b regardless of a’s status A newline usually behaves like the semicolon here: the next command still runs after an earlier failure. That is why a script ending with echo 'Done' can print a reassuring message after a failed copy.

title: 6.2 Exit Codes & Chaining
text: mkdir new-folder && cd new-folder Only enter the folder if creating it succeeded If mkdir fails because the name already exists, this form will not enter it. That may be exactly what you want for a fresh workspace. If existing directories are acceptable, mkdir -p expresses that different intention. a && b || c is not a general if/else statement. The fallback can run when either a fails or b fails . It can also hide an earlier failure if c succeeds. For more than a small chain, an explicit condition is easier to read. Try it: run the check before the next step Start with false && ./deploy.sh : the simulated deploy should not run. Then inspect the supplied scripts and use ./tests.sh && ./deploy.sh . The supplied tests succeed. Here “deploy” creates a marker file in the sandbox; it does not upload a site. Arguments: use the same script on another folder In ./backup.sh notes , the word notes is an argument . Inside the script, $1 holds the first argument. $2 holds the second. Quotes keep an argument with spaces together.

title: 6.2 Exit Codes & Chaining
text: #!/usr/bin/env bash mkdir -p "$HOME/backups" && cp -R "$1" "$HOME/backups/" Contents of backup.sh · a small argument exercise This version creates the backup folder and only copies if that step succeeds. The quoted "$1" is the source folder. Try it as ./backup.sh notes ; a folder named My Notes would be passed as ./backup.sh "My Notes" . This short teaching version assumes one existing source and an appropriate destination. It does not check missing arguments or preserve an earlier copy under a new name. Those are the next improvements—not details to leave to luck in a reusable script. Try it: choose the source when you run the script Use the file editor to create backup.sh with the argument version above. Save, read, add owner execution, run it on notes, and verify the copied files under backups/notes. Real Bash: make a decision with if The following examples use Bash features beyond the browser simulator. Practise them in a new folder on your own computer, using only files you created for this exercise. if [ -f notes.txt ]; then echo "The note exists" else echo "Create notes.txt first" fi Real Bash · run one branch according to a file check if runs a test command.

title: 6.2 Exit Codes & Chaining
text: If it succeeds, Bash runs the commands after then; otherwise it runs the else branch. fi ends the condition. The spaces inside [ -f notes.txt ] are required: the brackets and their arguments are separate words. -f checks for a regular file. -d checks for a directory. ! negates a result. These tests establish a particular fact; file existence alone does not prove that its contents are correct. Try both branches: run the example with no notes.txt, create it with touch, then run the example again. You should know which branch will run before pressing Enter. Real Bash: repeat a small task with a loop for plant in basil mint thyme; do printf 'Remember to water %s\n' "$plant" done Real Bash · one message for each plant for takes the values after in one at a time. On each pass, plant holds the next value. The commands between do and done run once for that value. The quoted variable remains one argument even when the value contains spaces. Add "lemon balm" to the list and predict how many lines will print. It should produce one line for that two-word plant, not two separate plants. Inside a script, "$@" means all its arguments, preserving each one as a separate word.

title: 6.2 Exit Codes & Chaining
text:
This is useful when repeating work over filenames: #!/usr/bin/env bash for path in "$@"; do printf 'You supplied: %s
' "$path" done Real Bash · contents of show-paths.sh Save the file, then try bash show-paths.sh notes.txt "My Notes.txt" . It should print two supplied paths. This demonstration only prints names; add file-changing work after you have verified the selection. Real Bash: a copy script that checks its assumptions Now combine the pieces into one useful routine. This script accepts a source folder and a new destination name. It refuses to overwrite an existing destination and only announces completion after the copy succeeds. #!/usr/bin/env bash # Usage: ./backup-safe.sh SOURCE_FOLDER NEW_DESTINATION if [ "$#" -ne 2 ]; then printf 'Usage: %s SOURCE_FOLDER NEW_DESTINATION
' "$0" >&2 exit 2 fi source_folder="$1" destination="$2" if [ ! -d "$source_folder" ]; then printf 'Source is not a directory: %s
' "$source_folder" >&2 exit 1 fi if [ -e "$destination" ] || [ -L "$destination" ]; then printf 'Destination already exists: %s
' "$destination" >&2 exit 1 fi if ! cp -R -- "$source_folder" "$destination"; then printf 'Copy failed.

title: 6.2 Exit Codes & Chaining
text: Inspect the destination before retrying.\n' >&2 exit 1 fi printf 'Copied %s to %s\n' "$source_folder" "$destination" Real Bash · save as backup-safe.sh $# counts arguments. The first condition requires exactly two before reading them. $0 is the script’s name, used in the usage message. The next condition checks that the source is a directory. The destination check rejects existing files, folders, and symbolic links. exit 1 stops with failure; exit 2 reports incorrect usage in this script. >&2 sends the explanation to the error channel. The final condition checks the copy itself. -- ends cp’s options so a supplied name beginning with a dash is treated as a name. Use a few disposable files to verify its behavior. First read the script, check its syntax, then run it with explicit paths: bash -n backup-safe.sh mkdir practice-notes echo "basil" > practice-notes/seeds.txt bash backup-safe.sh practice-notes "practice copy" cat "practice copy/seeds.txt" Real terminal · expect the copied file to contain basil bash -n checks syntax without executing the script. It does not prove the logic is right. Run the same copy again: it should refuse the existing destination.

title: 6.2 Exit Codes & Chaining
text: Try a missing source, then no arguments: both should return a nonzero status and a helpful message. Check $? immediately after each run. A failed copy can leave a partial destination. Inspect it before retrying; the script deliberately does not remove it automatically. Keep the destination outside the source folder. For important backups, also consider retained versions, metadata, separate storage, and a tested restore process. Two other script forms you will encounter Command substitution: TODAY=$(date +%F) runs date and stores its printed date in TODAY. It is useful for names, but a date alone is not unique if you run the script twice in one day. Choose and check a destination deliberately. A here-document: an agent may create a whole file by feeding several lines into cat. The quoted delimiter below prevents variables in the body from expanding while the file is being written: cat <<'EOF' > greeting.sh #!/usr/bin/env bash echo "Hello from the garden" EOF Real Bash · creates greeting.sh, replacing it if it exists The final EOF is the delimiter, not part of the saved file. The body is still code to read before running.

title: 6.2 Exit Codes & Chaining
text: The sandbox does not implement here-documents or command substitution. A useful script has a clear input, a clear result, and a clear response to failure. You do not need to make it short. Make it understandable enough that tomorrow you can explain each step.

title: Part 7 · Text Surgery
text: The café has run out of mango. Its menu needs kiwi instead. Let’s make that change without rewriting the whole file—or losing the original while we experiment. sed transforms text as it reads it. The basic commands here print the changed text while leaving the input file alone. Later, we’ll deliberately save a new file or edit an existing one. awk will help when the text is arranged into fields.

title: 7.1 Find & Replace
text: Suppose menu.txt contains this one line: mango smoothie — mango, ice, lime Example menu.txt Ask sed to substitute kiwi for mango: sed 's/mango/kiwi/' menu.txt kiwi smoothie — mango, ice, lime Only the first mango on the line changed. Add g to replace every match on each line: sed 's/mango/kiwi/g' menu.txt kiwi smoothie — kiwi, ice, lime s Substitute mango Find this pattern kiwi Replace with this g Every match on the line Now run cat menu.txt . The file should still say mango. sed printed a different version; it did not save that version over your input. To keep the result as a separate file, add redirection: sed 's/mango/kiwi/g' menu.txt > kiwi-menu.txt cat kiwi-menu.txt cat menu.txt Save a new version, then inspect both files Choose a destination different from the source. sed ... menu.txt > menu.txt can empty menu.txt before sed reads it. Redirection is handled by the shell, so that mistake happens before the text transformation. Know what the pattern means The find part is a regular expression, like grep without -F. It can match inside a larger word. The g means all matches on each line ; sed already processes every line by default.

title: 7.1 Find & Replace
text: Neither option means “only complete words.” A dot has a special pattern meaning. To match the literal text plan.md, use plan\.md in a sed pattern. The replacement has special characters too: & inserts the matched text. Do not assume arbitrary search and replacement strings can be pasted into this syntax unchanged. A different delimiter can make paths easier to read sed 's|/old/garden|/new/garden|g' paths.txt Use a vertical bar as sed’s separator The vertical bars here are inside quotes, so they belong to sed’s substitution syntax. A vertical bar outside quotes is the shell’s pipe. Changing the delimiter makes paths more readable; it does not make the search pattern literal. Case-insensitive sed flags vary between implementations. For portable simple matching, spell out the needed alternatives or inspect your system’s sed manual before using extensions such as I. Try it: make the kiwi menu The playground’s menu has several lines, and one has two mangos. Create kiwi-menu.txt with every intended substitution. Inspect the new menu and confirm menu.txt still contains the original.

title: 7.2 Line Surgery
text: A noisy log can be easier to read if you leave out routine DEBUG messages. In this command, /DEBUG/ chooses matching lines and d drops them from the output: sed '/DEBUG/d' app.log Preview the log without DEBUG lines The original log stays unchanged. To retain this filtered version, redirect it into a different name such as clean.log. One input line Read the next line /DEBUG/ Does the pattern match? d If yes, omit it; otherwise print it The selection before an action is called an address . It can be a line number, a range, or a pattern: Command What is omitted from the output sed '3d' notes.txt Line 3 sed '2,5d' notes.txt Lines 2 through 5, inclusive sed '$d' notes.txt The last line sed '/DEBUG/d' app.log Lines matching the regular expression DEBUG Print only a selected range sed -n '2,5p' notes.txt Show only lines 2 through 5 -n turns off sed’s automatic printing; p explicitly prints the selected lines. Without -n, those selected lines would normally be printed twice. The options and the little sed program have different jobs. You can also limit a substitution: sed '2s/mango/kiwi/g' menu.txt changes matches on line 2 only.

title: 7.2 Line Surgery
text: sed '/smoothie/s/mango/kiwi/g' menu.txt changes matches only on lines containing smoothie. Try a variation: print one numbered line, then a three-line range. Compare each result with the original. A precise selection is more useful than a shorter-looking command. Try it: keep the useful log Save a clean.log without DEBUG lines. Check that INFO and ERROR lines remain and that app.log has not changed. A filtered report is not a replacement for the original diagnostic record.

title: 7.3 Editing in Place
text: Sometimes you want the existing file to contain the new text. The option -i asks sed to edit a file in place. That changes the file you named, rather than merely printing a result. Begin with one file and preview the transformation without -i. Check that the chosen backup name does not already contain a version you need. Then the form -i.bak edits while saving a copy under a .bak name: sed 's/http:/https:/g' config.yml ls -a sed -i.bak 's/http:/https:/g' config.yml diff config.yml.bak config.yml Preview, check the backup name, edit, compare Here config.yml contains the edited text, and config.yml.bak contains the text from just before this edit. Repeating the command can replace that .bak file. It is one saved version, not an unlimited undo history. Read the diff before deciding the edit is finished diff compares two files. In its normal output, lines beginning < came from the first file, and lines beginning > came from the second. On a real terminal, diff -u gives a common format with surrounding context. No differences normally means no output and status 0. Status 1 means differences were found; that is not itself a broken comparison. A higher status indicates trouble comparing.

title: 7.3 Editing in Place
text: This is a useful example of why an exit status belongs to the command’s own rules. If you want to restore the original, inspect the backup, then deliberately copy it back with cp config.yml.bak config.yml . This replaces the edited version. Keep a separate copy of either version if you may need both later. The joined backup form -i.bak works with the common GNU and BSD sed versions used in this course. Bare -i behaves differently: GNU sed permits it without a backup, while BSD sed expects a following backup suffix, which may be an empty string. macOS does not force you to keep a backup. If a file contains a secret, a .bak copy may still contain that secret. Removing it from the edited file does not remove every copy. Review what the backup actually holds before sharing the folder. Try it: review a proposed edit The activity proposes replacing http: with https: in two configuration files. Read them, preview the result, and keep their originals using the requested backup suffix. A text change alone does not configure encryption on a server or prove that the new address works; this exercise checks the edit itself.

title: 7.4 Columns & awk
text: A plain text table might separate its values with spaces. For example: basil 3 sunny mint 5 shade thyme 2 sunny Example plants.txt · name, quantity, location awk normally separates each line into fields at runs of whitespace. $1 is the first field, $2 the second, and $0 the whole line. awk '{print $1}' plants.txt basil mint thyme awk '{print $1, $3}' plants.txt basil sunny mint shade thyme sunny The braces contain an action. print prints the fields you name; the comma between fields inserts an output separator, a space by default. The shell’s single quotes keep the awk program intact. The $1 here belongs to awk , not to the shell script argument from Part 6. Double-quoting this program can let the shell replace $1 before awk sees it. Keep these awk programs in single quotes. Select rows as well as fields awk '/sunny/ {print $1}' plants.txt basil thyme The pattern before the braces selects matching lines; the action only runs for those lines. This pattern matches sunny anywhere on the line. It is not yet a condition saying “the third field is exactly sunny.” Choose a different separator -F, tells awk to split fields at commas.

title: 7.4 Columns & awk
text: That is useful for a deliberately simple table with no quoted commas or embedded newlines: awk -F, '{print $2}' signups.csv cut -d, -f2 signups.csv Two ways to select field two from a simple unquoted comma table These agree for the practice file. They do not implement general CSV parsing. A value such as "Lovelace, Ada" contains a comma inside one quoted field; a plain split treats it as two. Use a CSV-aware tool or library for such data instead of adding guesses to this pipeline. For aligned text with varying numbers of spaces, awk’s default whitespace splitting is often convenient. cut is useful when a specific single character is truly the separator. Inspect the actual input before choosing. Real awk: add up a numeric field awk '{total += $2} END {print total}' plants.txt Real terminal · the quantities above total 10 This adds field two into a variable named total for every line. The END action runs once after the input ends and prints the total. It assumes field two contains valid numbers and there is no header row. The sandbox’s awk models basic field printing and pattern filters, not the full awk language.

title: 7.4 Columns & awk
text: Try it: extract the email field Read signups.csv, choose the separator, and save its second field as emails.txt. This practice includes the header name email in the output; a real mailing workflow would handle the header and validate addresses separately. No messages are sent. You can now search a file, preview a transformation, save a separate result, and inspect a deliberate edit. When a command gets harder to read, slow it down into those same steps.

title: Part 8 · Processes & Ports
text: A command does not always finish straight away. A server waits for requests. A log viewer waits for new lines. A download may still be working. The useful question is: what is running, and do I want it to keep running? In this chapter you will get your prompt back, identify a running program, and resolve a port conflict without guessing. The practice activities use simulated processes. The short native exercises are for your own terminal.

title: 8.1 Everything Is a Process
text: A process is a running instance of a program. Opening an editor starts a process. Running a second copy starts another. The operating system gives each one a number called its process ID , or PID. A filename tells you where a program is stored. A PID tells you which running instance you are looking at. Deleting a program's file is not the normal way to stop it. Run ps aux to see a broad process list on macOS or Linux. Its columns vary, so start with only three: the owner, PID, and command. CPU usage is another useful clue when the machine feels busy. ps aux USER PID %CPU COMMAND vibe 1024 0.0 bash vibe 400 0.4 node server.js vibe 437 97.4 spinner.sh --forever Example: a shortened process list In this example, process 437 is using a lot of CPU. That is a reason to investigate, not proof that it is broken: useful work can be expensive too. Read the command and owner before deciding what to stop. Your machine will have different PIDs, and a number can be reused after its process ends. To narrow a long list, try ps aux | grep server . The search command itself may appear in the results. Inspect the whole line instead of copying the first number you see.

title: 8.1 Everything Is a Process
text: A live view, when a snapshot is not enough top updates a process list while you watch. Press q to leave. The layout and sorting keys differ between macOS and Linux; the on-screen help or man top explains your version. A changing CPU value shows activity over time. It still does not tell you whether that activity is useful. Optional tools such as htop and btop offer more visual process views. Learn to identify the owner and command before using their stop buttons. A prettier list does not change what stopping a process does. Before continuing: in the example above, which number identifies the server? Which text tells you what it is running?

title: 8.2 Stopping Things
text: First try the smallest useful action. If the program is running in the terminal in front of you, press Ctrl+C . This sends an interrupt to the foreground process group. Many command-line programs respond by stopping. Some handle it differently, so look for the prompt to return. Try in your terminal: run sleep 30 . This program waits for 30 seconds and prints nothing. While you wait, press Ctrl+C. Your prompt should return early. You stopped a waiting program; you did not delete a file. If the program lives in another terminal, you can find its PID and send a signal with kill . The name sounds harsher than the default action: kill 437 normally sends TERM, a request to terminate. That gives a cooperating program a chance to finish cleanup. For the sample list above, you would inspect process 437, send kill 437 , and inspect again. If it is gone, you are done. If you get “No such process,” it may already have finished. If you get “Operation not permitted,” check ownership. Do not immediately add sudo. kill -9 437 sends KILL. A process cannot catch this signal to clean up, so unsaved work may be lost. Use it only after identifying the process and giving a normal stop a chance.

title: 8.2 Stopping Things
text: Even KILL is not a guarantee that every entry vanishes instantly; some system states take time to resolve. Try it: Stop the runaway After the activity, explain what evidence made you choose that process. “It had the biggest number” is not enough; a PID is an identifier, not a danger score.

title: 8.3 Who's on Port 3000?
text: A server listens for connections at an address and a port . Think of the address as a building and the port as the place inside it where a particular service answers. Port 3000 is a common development choice; it is not a special kind of server. “Address already in use” often means another process is already listening on the address and port your new server requested. The exact rules include the network protocol, address, and socket settings. For everyday debugging, find the listener before changing anything. A repeatable port check In this course's playground, lsof -i :3000 identifies a simulated listener. On macOS or Linux with lsof installed, the more specific command below asks for TCP listeners and keeps addresses and port numbers numeric. Your terminal: inspect TCP port 3000 lsof -nP -iTCP:3000 -sTCP:LISTEN Read the command, owner, PID, and listening address. If it is your old server, return to its terminal and press Ctrl+C, or terminate its verified PID. Run the inspection again. An empty result means this check found no matching listener, subject to your permissions. Start the intended server and check its response.

title: 8.3 Who's on Port 3000?
text: If the existing listener is useful, leave it running and configure the new server to use another port. You are solving a conflict, not collecting processes to kill. If lsof is missing on Linux, ss -ltnp is a common alternative; read its local manual and note that process details can require additional permissions. Try it: Free port 3000 Why is “kill whatever uses port 3000” a weaker plan than “identify my old server, then stop it”?

title: 8.4 Background & Foreground
text: A foreground job owns your terminal while it runs. A background job lets the shell accept another command. Add & to start a job in the background; use jobs to see jobs tracked by this shell. Try in your terminal: run sleep 60 & , then jobs . You may see a job number such as [1] and a PID. They are different identifiers. The job number belongs to this shell; the PID belongs to the operating system. fg %1 brings job 1 to the foreground. Press Ctrl+C to stop the sleep.
